cards.explanation: The answer is mercy, friends. David's first words are “Have mercy on me, O God, according to Your loving devotion…” No excuses and no warm-up speech. He leans on God's loving devotion and great compassion, and he asks.
The answer is False. David says, “For I know my transgressions, and my sin is always before me.” There's no fog in that sentence. He knows what he did and he doesn't dodge it.

The answer is God, friends. David says, “Against You, You only, have I sinned and done what is evil in Your sight…” He's praying to God, so he says it right to His face. He doesn't hide behind a long explanation either.

The answer is True. David says God will be “…proved right when You speak and blameless when You judge.” He isn't arguing his case or hunting for a loophole. He says God is in the right, and he's speaking to God Himself.

The answer is False. David says, “Surely I was brought forth in iniquity; I was sinful when my mother conceived me.” He doesn't claim a clean record up to some point. He traces it all the way back to the start.

The answer is in the inmost being, friends. David says, “Surely You desire truth in the inmost being…” That's the deep inside, the part nobody else sees. And he adds that God teaches him wisdom in the inmost place.

The answer is False. David says, “Purify me with hyssop, and I will be clean…” He doesn't leave room for a stubborn spot. We've all scrubbed a shirt and still found the mark, but David isn't talking about that kind of wash.

The answer is joy and gladness, friends. David prays, “Let me hear joy and gladness; let the bones You have crushed rejoice.” His bones are crushed and he still asks for joy. I think that's how much he wants God to restore him.

The answer is sins, friends. David says, “Hide Your face from my sins and blot out all my iniquities.” Notice it's his own sins he wants hidden, not anybody else's. And he asks again for them to be blotted out, the same word he used at the start.

The answer is a clean heart, friends. David prays, “Create in me a clean heart, O God, and renew a right spirit within me.” That's a request for something new on the inside. It goes deeper than washing the outside.

The answer is God's presence, friends. David prays, “Cast me not away from Your presence…” Of everything he could be afraid of losing, he names being near God. I think that tells you what matters most to him right now.

The answer is True. In the same breath David says, “take not Your Holy Spirit from me.” That's his second request, right alongside not being cast away from God's presence. Two prayers, one right after the other.

The answer is the joy of His salvation, friends. David asks, “Restore to me the joy of Your salvation…” The word restore tells you he's had that joy before. I bet he's thinking about how much he's missing it.

The answer is that sinners will return to God, friends. David says, “Then I will teach transgressors Your ways, and sinners will return to You.” He wants to help other people find their way back. Someone asking God for mercy and then pointing others to that same God, that's the picture.

The answer is True. David prays, “Deliver me from bloodguilt, O God, the God of my salvation, and my tongue will sing of Your righteousness.” He ties the singing to being delivered. It's a quiet kind of promise.

The answer is False. David says, “For You do not delight in sacrifice, or I would bring it; You take no pleasure in burnt offerings.” He says he would bring one if that's what God wanted. Then he tells us what God does want in the next verse.

The answer is a broken spirit, friends. David says, “The sacrifices of God are a broken spirit…” After saying God takes no pleasure in burnt offerings, he points to something inside a person. It's an honest, humble spirit before God.
The answer is False. David says, “a broken and a contrite heart, O God, You will not despise.” Whoever comes to God with a heart like that, David says, He won't look down on it.

The answer is Jerusalem, friends. David prays, “In Your good pleasure, cause Zion to prosper; build up the walls of Jerusalem.” After all that praying about himself, he ends by praying for the city. His prayer opens up wider.

The answer is righteous, friends. David says, “Then You will delight in righteous sacrifices, in whole burnt offerings…” Notice that word then. After the broken spirit and the prayer for Jerusalem, he says God will delight in them.
